questions.enonce_markdown: A complex number $z$ satisfies the equation $\dfrac{z}{z + 2} = 2 - i$. Express $z$ in the form $a + bi$, where $a$ and $b$ are real constants. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Multiply both sides by $z + 2$ (note $z \neq -2$):
$$z = (2 - i)(z + 2) = (2 - i)z + 2(2 - i).$$
Collect the terms in $z$ on the left:
$$z - (2 - i)z = 4 - 2i \;\Longrightarrow\; (-1 + i)\,z = 4 - 2i \;\Longrightarrow\; z = \frac{4 - 2i}{-1 + i}.$$
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $-1 - i$ of the denominator ($(-1 + i)(-1 - i) = 1 + 1 = 2$):
$$z = \frac{(4 - 2i)(-1 - i)}{2} = \frac{-4 - 4i + 2i + 2i^2}{2} = \frac{-4 - 2i - 2}{2} = \frac{-6 - 2i}{2} = -3 - i.$$
$$\boxed{z = -3 - i}$$
**Check:** $z + 2 = -1 - i$ and $(2 - i)(-1 - i) = -2 - 2i + i + i^2 = -3 - i = z$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The vector equations of two lines are given by $\mathbf{r} = 3\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} + \lambda(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k})$ and $\mathbf{r} = 3\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k} + \mu(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k})$.

(a) Find the vector normal to the plane containing both lines. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The direction vectors of the lines are $\mathbf{d}_1 = 2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{d}_2 = \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$. They are not parallel (no scalar $c$ gives $\mathbf{d}_1 = c\,\mathbf{d}_2$).

**The lines meet, so they lie in one plane.** Equate the position vectors:
$$3 + 2\lambda = 3 + \mu, \qquad 6 + 3\lambda = -1 - 2\mu, \qquad 1 - \lambda = 4 + \mu.$$
The first gives $\mu = 2\lambda$. The second then gives $6 + 3\lambda = -1 - 4\lambda$, so $\lambda = -1$ and $\mu = -2$. The third is satisfied: $1 - (-1) = 2$ and $4 + (-2) = 2$. The lines intersect at the point $(1, 3, 2)$, so they are coplanar and the plane containing both is determined.

**Normal vector.** A vector normal to the plane is perpendicular to both directions, so take the cross product:
$$\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2 = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{i}\big(3 \cdot 1 - (-1)(-2)\big) - \mathbf{j}\big(2 \cdot 1 - (-1)(1)\big) + \mathbf{k}\big(2(-2) - 3 \cdot 1\big)$$
$$= \mathbf{i}(3 - 2) - \mathbf{j}(2 + 1) + \mathbf{k}(-4 - 3) = \mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} - 7\mathbf{k}.$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} - 7\mathbf{k}\ \ (\text{or any non-zero multiple})}$$
**Check:** $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_1 = 2 - 9 + 7 = 0$ and $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_2 = 1 + 6 - 7 = 0$.

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) Obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane containing both lines. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The plane has normal $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} - 7\mathbf{k}$ (part (a)) and passes through the point $(3, 6, 1)$ of the first line. Its equation is $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}$ with $\mathbf{a} = 3\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$:
$$x - 3y - 7z = 3 - 18 - 7 = -22.$$
$$\boxed{x - 3y - 7z + 22 = 0}$$
**Check** (both lines lie in the plane):
- point $(3, -1, 4)$ of the second line: $3 + 3 - 28 = -22$, so it lies on the plane;
- intersection point $(1, 3, 2)$: $1 - 9 - 14 = -22$, so it lies on the plane;
- both direction vectors are perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$ (part (a)), so every point of each line satisfies the equation.
